questions.q: Let $\bar{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $\bar{c}=5 \hat{i}-3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and if $\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\bar{a}$ then $|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|=$
questions.solution:
Given vectors: $\bar{a} = \hat{\imath} + \hat{\jmath} - \hat{k}$ and $\bar{c} = 5\hat{\imath} - 3\hat{\jmath} + 2\hat{k}$, with $\bar{b} \times \bar{c} = \bar{a}$.

The magnitude of $\bar{a}$ is $|\bar{a}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + (-1)^2} = \sqrt{3}$, and $|\bar{c}| = \sqrt{5^2 + (-3)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{38}$.

Using the identity $|\bar{X} \times \bar{Y}|^2 = |\bar{X}|^2 |\bar{Y}|^2 - (\bar{X} \cdot \bar{Y})^2$ with $\bar{X} = \bar{b}$ and $\bar{Y} = \bar{c}$ gives $|\bar{b}|^2 |\bar{c}|^2 - (\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c})^2 = |\bar{a}|^2$.

Substituting known values: $|\bar{b}|^2 \cdot 38 - (\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c})^2 = 3$.

Testing $|\bar{b}| = \sqrt{114}$ yields $(\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c})^2 = 38 \cdot 114 - 3 = 4329$, a positive real number, confirming feasibility.

The final answer is $\boxed{\sqrt{114}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ then a vector $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ such that $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}=3$ is
questions.solution:
Finding vector $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ from given conditions:

Let $\overline{\mathrm{c}} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. Given $\bar{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}} = \hat{j} - \hat{k}$, with $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}} = 3$ and $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}} = \overline{\mathrm{b}}$.

The dot product yields $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}} = x + y + z = 3$.

The cross product $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ evaluates to $(z - y)\hat{i} - (z - x)\hat{j} + (y - x)\hat{k}$, which equals $\overline{\mathrm{b}} = 0\hat{i} + 1\hat{j} - 1\hat{k}$. Component comparison gives $z = y$, $x - z = 1$, and $y - x = -1$.

Substituting $y = z$ into the dot product: $x + 2z = 3$. With $x - z = 1$, subtracting yields $3z = 2$, so $z = \frac{2}{3}$ and $x = \frac{5}{3}$. Since $y = z$, $y = \frac{2}{3}$.

Thus, $\overline{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{5}{3}\hat{i} + \frac{2}{3}\hat{j} + \frac{2}{3}\hat{k}$, matching option A.

Final answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
A tetrahedron has vertices $O(0,0,0) A(1,2,1) B(2,1,3) C(-1,1,2)$.
Then the angle between the faces $O A B$ and $A B C$ will be
questions.solution:
To determine the angle between the faces of the tetrahedron with vertices $O(0,0,0)$, $A(1,2,1)$, $B(2,1,3)$, and $C(-1,1,2)$, the normal vectors to each face are computed using the cross product.

The normal vector $\mathrm{n_1}$ to face $OAB$ is given by $\mathrm{OA} \times \mathrm{OB}$, where $\mathrm{OA} = (1,2,1)$ and $\mathrm{OB} = (2,1,3)$.
This yields $\mathrm{n_1} = (5, -1, -3)$.

Similarly, the normal vector $\mathrm{n_2}$ to face $ABC$ is found from $\mathrm{AB} \times \mathrm{AC}$, with $\mathrm{AB} = (1, -1, 2)$ and $\mathrm{AC} = (-2, -1, 1)$.
The result is $\mathrm{n_2} = (1, -5, -3)$.

The angle $\theta$ between the faces is the angle between their normals, given by $\cos \theta = \frac{\mathrm{n_1} \cdot \mathrm{n_2}}{|\mathrm{n_1}| |\mathrm{n_2}|}$.
The dot product $\mathrm{n_1} \cdot \mathrm{n_2} = 5 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot (-5) + (-3) \cdot (-3) = 19$.
Both magnitudes are $\sqrt{35}$, so $\cos \theta = \frac{19}{35}$.

The angle is $\theta = \cos^{-1} \left( \frac{19}{35} \right)$, corresponding to option A.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The position vectors of the points $A, B, C$ are $\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}, \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ respectively. If $A$ is chosen as the origin, then the cross product of position vectors of $B$ and $C$ are
questions.solution:
Given position vectors:
$\vec{r}_A = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$
$\vec{r}_B = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$
$\vec{r}_C = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$

With A as the origin, the position vectors relative to A are:
$\vec{AB} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A = (1-1)\hat{i} + (1-2)\hat{j} + (1-(-1))\hat{k} = -\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$
$\vec{AC} = \vec{r}_C - \vec{r}_A = (2-1)\hat{i} + (3-2)\hat{j} + (2-(-1))\hat{k} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$

The cross product is evaluated as:

$\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-3 - 2) - \hat{j}(0 - 2) + \hat{k}(0 - (-1)) = -5\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$

This result corresponds exactly with option A.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the area of a parallelogram whose diagonals are represented by vectors $3 \hat{i}+\lambda \hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{117}}{2}$ sq. units, then $\lambda=$
questions.solution:
Given diagonal vectors are $\vec{d_1} = 3\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{d_2} = \hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$. The area of the parallelogram formed by diagonals $\vec{d_1}$ and $\vec{d_2}$ is $\frac{1}{2} |\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}|$.

Compute the cross product: $\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2} = (3\lambda + 4)\hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + (-6 - \lambda)\hat{k}$.

Its magnitude is $|\vec{d_1} \times \vec{d_2}| = \sqrt{(3\lambda + 4)^2 + 49 + (-6 - \lambda)^2} = \sqrt{10\lambda^2 + 36\lambda + 101}$.

Given the area is $\frac{\sqrt{117}}{2}$, equate:
$\frac{\sqrt{117}}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{10\lambda^2 + 36\lambda + 101}$
Multiplying both sides by 2 and squaring: $117 = 10\lambda^2 + 36\lambda + 101$.

Rearranged as the quadratic $5\lambda^2 + 18\lambda - 8 = 0$. Solving, the discriminant is $\sqrt{324 + 160} = \sqrt{484} = 22$, so $\lambda = \frac{-18 \pm 22}{10}$, yielding $\lambda = \frac{2}{5}$ or $\lambda = -4$.

Among the options, $\lambda = -4$ corresponds to choice D.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: if $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ are non coplanar unit vectors such that $\bar{a} \times(\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{b}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}}{\sqrt{2}}$ Then the angle between $\bar{a}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ is
questions.solution:
Given $\bar{a} \times (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = \frac{\bar{b} + \bar{c}}{\sqrt{2}}$, expand the triple product using the identity $\bar{a} \times (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})\bar{b} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})\bar{c}$.

This yields $(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})\bar{b} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})\bar{c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bar{b} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bar{c}$.

Since $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ are non-coplanar unit vectors and thus linearly independent, equate coefficients:

$\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$-(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Solving gives $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

For unit vectors, the dot product equals $\cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$. Thus, $\cos \theta = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{4}$.

The angle between $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ is $\frac{3\pi}{4}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}=2 \hat{i}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}=3 \hat{i}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}$, then vector $\overline{\mathrm{p}}$ satisfying $\overline{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \bar{a}=0$ and $\overline{\mathrm{p}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ is
questions.solution:
The condition $\overline{p} \times \overline{b} = \overline{c} \times \overline{b}$ implies that $(\overline{p} - \overline{c}) \times \overline{b} = 0$, so $\overline{p} - \overline{c}$ is parallel to $\overline{b}$. Therefore, $\overline{p} = \overline{c} + \lambda \overline{b}$ for some scalar $\lambda$.

Substituting the given $\overline{c} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\overline{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{k}$, we obtain:

$\overline{p} = (3 + 2\lambda)\hat{i} - \hat{j} + (1 - \lambda)\hat{k}$

Applying the condition $\overline{p} \cdot \overline{a} = 0$ with $\overline{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$:

$(3 + 2\lambda)(1) + (-1)(1) = 0$

$2\lambda + 2 = 0$

$\lambda = -1$

Substituting back:

$\overline{p} = (3 - 2)\hat{i} - \hat{j} + (1 + 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$

The result matches option D.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}=2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}=\hat{i}-2 \hat{j}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}=-\hat{i}+4 \hat{j}+3 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and if $\overline{\mathrm{d}}$ is vector perpendicular to both $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}, \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{d}}=18$, then $|\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}}|^2=$
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $\bar{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, and $\bar{c} = -\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

A vector perpendicular to both $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$ is given by their cross product: $\bar{b} \times \bar{c} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.

Since $\bar{d}$ is perpendicular to both $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$, it must be parallel to $\bar{b} \times \bar{c}$, so $\bar{d} = \lambda(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k})$ for some scalar $\lambda$.

Using $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{d} = 18$ gives: $\lambda((2)(2) + (3)(-1) + (4)(2)) = 18$, $\lambda(9) = 18$, $\lambda = 2$.

Thus $\bar{d} = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$.

The magnitude squared of $\bar{a} \times \bar{d}$ can be found using the identity: $|\bar{a} \times \bar{d}|^{2} = |\bar{a}|^{2}|\bar{d}|^{2} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{d})^{2}$.

With $|\bar{a}|^{2} = 2^{2} + 3^{2} + 4^{2} = 29$, $|\bar{d}|^{2} = 4^{2} + (-2)^{2} + 4^{2} = 36$, and $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{d} = 18$, we obtain: $|\bar{a} \times \bar{d}|^{2} = (29)(36) - (18)^{2} = 1044 - 324 = 720$.

Alternatively, computing $\bar{a} \times \bar{d} = 20\hat{i} + 8\hat{j} - 16\hat{k}$ gives the same result: $(20)^{2} + (8)^{2} + (-16)^{2} = 720$.

Final answer: $720$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ be three vectors such that $\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\overline{0},|\bar{a}|=3,|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}|=4$, $|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=5$, then $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \bar{c}+\overline{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \bar{a}=$
questions.solution:
Given that $\bar{a} + \bar{b} + \bar{c} = \bar{0}$ and $|\bar{a}| = 3$, $|\bar{b}| = 4$, $|\bar{c}| = 5$, to find $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a}$.

The magnitude of the sum squared expands as $|\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$.

Since $\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c} = \bar{0}$, the left side is zero: $0 = 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$

$0 = 9 + 16 + 25 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$

$0 = 50 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$

Solving gives $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a} = -25$

Final answer: $\boxed{-25}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3 \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{1}{7}(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-6 \hat{\mathrm{k}})$ then the value of $(2 \bar{a}-\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \cdot((\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times(\bar{a}+2 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}))=$
questions.solution:
Given the expression $E = (2 \bar{a} - \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \cdot ((\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times (\bar{a} + 2 \overline{\mathrm{b}}))$, applying the vector triple product identity $(\vec{X} \times \vec{Y}) \times \vec{Z} = (\vec{X} \cdot \vec{Z})\vec{Y} - (\vec{Y} \cdot \vec{Z})\vec{X}$ with $\vec{X} = \bar{a}$, $\vec{Y} = \overline{\mathrm{b}}$, $\vec{Z} = \bar{a} + 2 \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ yields:

$(\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times (\bar{a} + 2 \overline{\mathrm{b}}) = (|\bar{a}|^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}}))\overline{\mathrm{b}} - ((\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}}) + 2|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2)\bar{a}$

Substituting back and computing the dot product with $2\bar{a} - \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ gives:

$E = (2K_1 + K_2)(\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}}) - 2K_2|\bar{a}|^2 - K_1|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2$

where $K_1 = |\bar{a}|^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}})$ and $K_2 = \bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}} + 2|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2$.

After substitution and simplification, terms cancel to yield:

$E = 5[(\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}})^2 - |\bar{a}|^2|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2]$

Given $\bar{a} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3\hat{i} + \hat{k})$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{1}{7}(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k})$, the squared magnitudes are $|\bar{a}|^2 = 1$ and $|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2 = 1$, while their dot product is $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}} = 0$.

Thus, $E = 5(0 - 1) = -5$.

Final answer: $-5$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}, \overline{\mathrm{d}}$ are vectors such that $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}=2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}}=3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\lambda \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and if $\left|\begin{array}{cc}\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}} & \overline{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}} \\ \bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~d}} & \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~d}}\end{array}\right|=0$, then $\lambda=$
questions.solution:
A fundamental identity in vector algebra relates mixed scalar and vector products:

$\left|\begin{array}{cc}\bar{a} \cdot \overline{c} & \overline{b} \cdot \overline{c} \\ \bar{a} \cdot \overline{d} & \overline{b} \cdot \overline{d}\end{array}\right| = (\bar{a} \times \overline{b}) \cdot (\overline{c} \times \overline{d})$

Given that this determinant equals zero, the dot product of the cross products must also vanish:

$(\bar{a} \times \overline{b}) \cdot (\overline{c} \times \overline{d}) = 0$

Substituting the provided expressions $\bar{a} \times \overline{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\overline{c} \times \overline{d} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \lambda\hat{k}$ yields:

$(2)(3) + (3)(2) + (-1)(\lambda) = 0$

$6 + 6 - \lambda = 0$

$\lambda = 12$

The correct choice is option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ be three vectors such that $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ and $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c}=0$. If the length of projection vector of the vector $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ on the vector $\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is $l$, then the value of $3 l^2$ is
questions.solution:
Given vectors:

$\bar{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

$\bar{c} = \hat{j} - \hat{k}$


The condition $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = 0$ is satisfied since $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{c}$ are orthogonal.


Let $\bar{d} = \bar{a} \times \bar{c}$. Using the determinant form:

$\bar{d} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$


The magnitude is $|\bar{d}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + 1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{6}$.


The projection length of $\bar{b}$ on $\bar{d}$ is $l = \frac{|\bar{b} \cdot \bar{d}|}{|\bar{d}|}$.


Using the scalar triple product property:

$\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = -[\bar{a}\ \bar{b}\ \bar{c}] = -(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot \bar{c}$


Given $\bar{a} \times \bar{b} = \bar{c}$, this becomes $-\bar{c} \cdot \bar{c} = -|\bar{c}|^2$.


Since $|\bar{c}|^2 = 1^2 + (-1)^2 = 2$, we have $\bar{b} \cdot \bar{d} = -2$.


The projection length is $l = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}$ and $3l^2 = 3 \cdot \frac{4}{6} = 2$.


The final result is $2$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The area of the rectangle having vertices $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}, \mathrm{S}$ with position vectors $-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k},-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ respectively is
questions.solution:
Position vectors in 3D space:

Given vertices: $\vec{P} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{Q} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{R} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{S} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

Adjacent sides from vertex P: $\vec{PQ} = \vec{Q} - \vec{P} = 2\hat{i}$, $\vec{PS} = \vec{S} - \vec{P} = -2\hat{j}$

These vectors are orthogonal with magnitudes $|\vec{PQ}| = 2$ and $|\vec{PS}| = 2$, confirming rectangular geometry.

The area follows from the cross product magnitude or product of adjacent sides:

$|\vec{PQ} \times \vec{PS}| = |(2\hat{i}) \times (-2\hat{j})| = 4$

$\boxed{4\text{ square units}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ are three vectors such that $|\bar{a}|=\sqrt{31}, 4|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}|=|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=2$ and $2(\bar{a} \times \bar{b})=3\left(\bar{c} \times \bar{a}\right.$ )and if the angle between $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$ is $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ then $\left|\frac{\bar{a} \times \bar{c}}{\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}}\right|^2=$
questions.solution:
Given vector magnitudes:

$|\bar{a}| = \sqrt{31}$

$|\bar{b}| = \frac{1}{2}$

$|\bar{c}| = 2$

The angle between $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$ is $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.

The vector relation $2(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) = 3(\bar{c} \times \bar{a})$ becomes $2(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) + 3(\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = \overline{0}$ after using $\bar{c} \times \bar{a} = -(\bar{a} \times \bar{c})$.

Factoring gives $\bar{a} \times (2\bar{b} + 3\bar{c}) = \overline{0}$, implying $2\bar{b} + 3\bar{c} = k\bar{a}$ for some scalar $k$.

The magnitude squared yields:

$|2\bar{b} + 3\bar{c}|^2 = 4|\bar{b}|^2 + 9|\bar{c}|^2 + 12(\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c}) = 4(\frac{1}{4}) + 9(4) + 12(-\frac{1}{2}) = 1 + 36 - 6 = 31$

Since $|k\bar{a}|^2 = k^2|\bar{a}|^2 = k^2 \cdot 31$, we find $k^2 = 1$, so $k = \pm 1$.

For both cases, $|\bar{a} \times \bar{c}|^2 = 4|\bar{b} \times \bar{c}|^2 = 4(|\bar{b}||\bar{c}|\sin\theta)^2 = 4(\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})^2 = 3$.

When $k = 1$, $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = 2|\bar{b}|^2 + 3(\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c}) = 2(\frac{1}{4}) + 3(-\frac{1}{2}) = -1$.

When $k = -1$, $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = -[2|\bar{b}|^2 + 3(\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c})] = 1$.

The expression simplifies to:

$\left|\frac{\bar{a} \times \bar{c}}{\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}}\right|^2 = \frac{|\bar{a} \times \bar{c}|^2}{(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})^2} = \frac{3}{1} = 3$

Final answer: $\boxed{3}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \bar{b}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and vector $\bar{c}$ be coplanar. If $\bar{c}$ is perpendicular to $\bar{a}$, then $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\bar{b}=\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-\hat{k}$, find vector $\bar{c} = x \hat{i} + y \hat{j} + z \hat{k}$ that is coplanar with $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ and perpendicular to $\bar{a}$.

Coplanarity requires $\bar{c} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) = 0$. Compute $\bar{a} \times \bar{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(-1 - 2) - \hat{j}(-2 - 1) + \hat{k}(4 - 1) = -3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

Dot product gives $-3x + 3y + 3z = 0$; dividing by 3 yields $-x + y + z = 0$.

Perpendicularity requires $\bar{c} \cdot \bar{a} = 0$, giving $2x + y + z = 0$.

Subtracting the first equation from the second: $(2x + y + z) - (-x + y + z) = 0 \implies 3x = 0 \implies x = 0$.

Substitute $x = 0$ into $-x + y + z = 0$ to get $y + z = 0$, so $z = -y$.

Thus, $\bar{c} = y(\hat{j} - \hat{k})$. Comparing with the options, $\boxed{\text{D}}$ gives $-\hat{j} + \hat{k} = -1(\hat{j} - \hat{k})$, which matches the form with $y = -1$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of integral values of $p$ for which the vector $(\mathrm{p}+1) \hat{i}-3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{p} \widehat{\mathrm{k}}, \mathrm{p} \hat{i}+(\mathrm{p}+1) \hat{\mathrm{j}}-3 \widehat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $-3 \hat{i}+\mathrm{p} \hat{\mathrm{j}}+(\mathrm{p}+1) \widehat{\mathrm{k}}$ are linearly dependent vectors, are
questions.solution:
The vectors are linearly dependent when their scalar triple product vanishes, which occurs when the determinant of their component matrix equals zero.

$\begin{vmatrix} p+1 & -3 & p \\ p & p+1 & -3 \\ -3 & p & p+1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant yields:

$(p+1)[(p+1)^2 + 3p] + 3[p(p+1) - 9] + p[p^2 + 3(p+1)] = 0$

Simplifying the expression:

$(p+1)(p^2 + 5p + 1) + 3p^2 + 3p - 27 + p^3 + 3p^2 + 3p = 0$

Combining like terms produces the cubic equation:

$2p^3 + 12p^2 + 12p - 26 = 0$

Dividing through by 2:

$p^3 + 6p^2 + 6p - 13 = 0$

Testing integer divisors of -13 reveals that $p = 1$ is a root, giving the factorization:

$(p-1)(p^2 + 7p + 13) = 0$

The quadratic factor $p^2 + 7p + 13$ has discriminant $\Delta = 49 - 52 = -3 \lt 0$, indicating no real roots.

Thus, the only integral solution is $p = 1$, corresponding to one integral value.

The final answer is $\boxed{B}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\overline{\mathrm{p}}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \quad \overline{\mathrm{q}}=\hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \quad \overline{\mathrm{r}}=4 \hat{i}-3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+7 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and a vector $\overline{\mathrm{m}}$ is such that $\overline{\mathrm{m}} \times \overline{\mathrm{q}}=\overline{\mathrm{r}} \times \overline{\mathrm{q}}, \overline{\mathrm{m}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{p}}=0$, then $\overline{\mathrm{m}}=\ldots$.
questions.solution:
Given vectors are: p$=2\hat{i}+\hat{k}$, q$=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, r$=4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$.

From the condition m × q $=$ r × q, we obtain $(\overline{m} - \overline{r}) \times \overline{q} = \overline{0}$. Since $\overline{q} \neq \overline{0}$, it follows that $\overline{m} - \overline{r}$ must be parallel to $\overline{q}$, so $\overline{m} = \overline{r} + \lambda \overline{q}$ for some scalar $\lambda$.

$\overline{m} = (4\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+7\hat{k}) + \lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}) = (4+\lambda)\hat{i} + (-3+\lambda)\hat{j} + (7+\lambda)\hat{k}$

Applying the condition $\overline{m} \cdot \overline{p} = 0$ yields:

$(4+\lambda)(2) + (-3+\lambda)(0) + (7+\lambda)(1) = 0$

$8 + 2\lambda + 7 + \lambda = 0$

$3\lambda + 15 = 0$

$\lambda = -5$

Substituting gives $\overline{m} = (-1)\hat{i} + (-8)\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, which corresponds to option C.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the area of parallelogram, whose diagonals are $\hat{i}-\hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and $2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+\alpha \hat{k}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{93}}{2}$ sq. unit, then $\alpha=$
questions.solution:
Given the diagonals of the parallelogram $\mathrm{d_1} = \hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\mathrm{d_2} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \alpha\hat{k}$, the area is determined by the formula $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} |\mathrm{d_1} \times \mathrm{d_2}|$.

The cross product evaluates to $\mathrm{d_1} \times \mathrm{d_2} = (-\alpha - 6)\hat{i} - (\alpha - 4)\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$.

Its magnitude is $|\mathrm{d_1} \times \mathrm{d_2}| = \sqrt{(\alpha + 6)^2 + (\alpha - 4)^2 + 25} = \sqrt{2\alpha^2 + 4\alpha + 77}$.

Given the area $\frac{\sqrt{93}}{2}$, we have $\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2\alpha^2 + 4\alpha + 77} = \frac{\sqrt{93}}{2}$, which simplifies to $\sqrt{2\alpha^2 + 4\alpha + 77} = \sqrt{93}$.

Squaring both sides yields $2\alpha^2 + 4\alpha + 77 = 93$, leading to $2\alpha^2 + 4\alpha - 16 = 0$.

Dividing by 2 gives $\alpha^2 + 2\alpha - 8 = 0$, which factors as $(\alpha + 4)(\alpha - 2) = 0$.

The solutions are $\alpha = -4$ and $\alpha = 2$, corresponding to option A.

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the lengths of three vectors $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ are 5,12,13 units respectively, and each one is perpendicular to the sum of the other two, then $|\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=\ldots \ldots$
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ with magnitudes $|\bar{a}| = 5$, $|\bar{b}| = 12$, and $|\bar{c}| = 13$, where each vector is perpendicular to the sum of the other two. This implies the dot products:

$\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b} + \bar{c}) = 0$, $\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} + \bar{c}) = 0$, and $\bar{c} \cdot (\bar{a} + \bar{b}) = 0$.

Expanding and summing these three equations yields:

$2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a}) = 0$,

so $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a} = 0$.

The magnitude squared of the resultant vector $\bar{R} = \bar{a} + \bar{b} + \bar{c}$ is:

$|\bar{R}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$.

Substituting the known values gives:

$|\bar{R}|^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 + 13^2 + 2(0) = 25 + 144 + 169 = 338$.

Therefore, $|\bar{R}| = \sqrt{338}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ are three unit vectors such that $|\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2+|\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2=8$, then $|\bar{a}+3 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}|^2+|\bar{a}+3 \overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2=$
questions.solution:
Given that $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ are unit vectors, their magnitudes satisfy $|\bar{a}| = |\bar{b}| = |\bar{c}| = 1$.

The equation $|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{a} + \bar{c}|^2 = 8$ expands to:

$(2 + 2\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + (2 + 2\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c}) = 8$

Simplifying yields:

$4 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{a} \cdot \bar{c}) = 8$

Thus $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = 2$

The expression $|\bar{a} + 3\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{a} + 3\bar{c}|^2$ becomes:

$(10 + 6\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + (10 + 6\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})$
$= 20 + 6(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})$

Substituting the previous result gives:

$20 + 6 \cdot 2 = 32$

Final Answer: $\boxed{32}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: $\bar{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\hat{\mathrm{k}}-\hat{i}$ then a unit vector $\overline{\mathrm{d}}$ such that $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{d}=0=[\bar{b} \bar{c} \bar{d}]$ is
questions.solution:
Let $\bar{d}=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j}+z\hat{k}$ be a unit vector orthogonal to $\bar{a}=\hat{i}-\hat{j}$ and coplanar with $\bar{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$, $\bar{c}=\hat{k}-\hat{i}$.

The orthogonality condition $\bar{a}\cdot\bar{d}=0$ gives $x-y=0$, so $x=y$.

The coplanarity of $\bar{b}$, $\bar{c}$, $\bar{d}$ is equivalent to $\left[\bar{b}\ \bar{c}\ \bar{d}\right]=0$, which implies $\bar{d}$ is orthogonal to $\bar{b}\times\bar{c}$.

Compute $\bar{b}\times\bar{c}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(1\cdot1-(-1)\cdot0)-\hat{j}(0\cdot1-(-1)\cdot(-1))+\hat{k}(0\cdot0-1\cdot(-1))=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$.

Then $\bar{d}\cdot(\bar{b}\times\bar{c})=x+y+z=0$. With $x=y$, we get $2x+z=0$, so $z=-2x$.

Thus $\bar{d}=x(\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k})$. The unit vector condition requires $|x|\sqrt{1^2+1^2+(-2)^2}=1$, so $|x|\sqrt{6}=1$ and $x=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$.

Therefore $\bar{d}=\pm\frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}}{\sqrt{6}}$, which corresponds to Option D.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the vectors $m \hat{i}+m \hat{j}+n \hat{k}, \hat{i}+\hat{k}, n \hat{i}+n \hat{j}+p \hat{k}$ lie in a plane then...
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\mathrm{a} = m \hat{i} + m \hat{j} + n \hat{k}$, $\mathrm{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{k}$, and $\mathrm{c} = n \hat{i} + n \hat{j} + p \hat{k}$, coplanarity requires the scalar triple product to vanish.

The determinant condition yields

$\begin{vmatrix} m & m & n \ 1 & 0 & 1 \ n & n & p \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding along the first row: $m(0 \cdot p - 1 \cdot n) - m(1 \cdot p - 1 \cdot n) + n(1 \cdot n - 0 \cdot n) = -mn - m(p - n) + n^2 = -mp + n^2 = 0$

This simplifies to $n^2 = mp$, indicating $m$, $n$, and $p$ form a geometric progression.

Among the options, only C satisfies this condition.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The area of a parallelogram whose diagonals are the vectors $2 \bar{a}-\bar{b}$ and $4 \bar{a}-5 \bar{b}$, where $\bar{a}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ are unit vectors forming an angle of $45^{\circ}$ is
questions.solution:
The diagonals of the parallelogram are given by $\bar{d}_1 = 2\bar{a} - \bar{b}$ and $\bar{d}_2 = 4\bar{a} - 5\bar{b}$, where $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ are unit vectors separated by $45^\circ$.

The area of a parallelogram with diagonals $\bar{d}_1$ and $\bar{d}_2$ is $\frac{1}{2}|\bar{d}_1 \times \bar{d}_2|$.

The cross product evaluates to:

$\bar{d}_1 \times \bar{d}_2 = (2\bar{a} - \bar{b}) \times (4\bar{a} - 5\bar{b}) = -10(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) + 4(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) = -6(\bar{a} \times \bar{b})$

Taking magnitude gives $|\bar{d}_1 \times \bar{d}_2| = 6|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|$.

Since $|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}| = |\bar{a}||\bar{b}|\sin(45^\circ) = 1 \times 1 \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, it follows that $|\bar{d}_1 \times \bar{d}_2| = \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}$.

The area is therefore $\frac{1}{2} \times 3\sqrt{2} = \frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

This matches option B.

There is nonzero vector $\bar{d}$ coplanar with $\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $2 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}-\overline{\mathrm{c}}$. If $\overline{\mathrm{d}} \cdot \bar{a}=1$, then $|\overline{\mathrm{d}}|^2=$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The value of $m \in \mathbb{R}$, when angle between the vectors $\bar{p}=m y \hat{i}-6 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k}$ and $\bar{q}=y \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+2 m y \hat{k}$ is obtuse angle, is
questions.solution:
To ensure the angle between vectors $\bar{p}=my\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\bar{q}=y\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2my\hat{k}$ is obtuse, the dot product must satisfy $\bar{p} \cdot \bar{q} \lt 0$. This gives:

$my^2 + 6my - 12 \lt 0$

For this quadratic inequality to hold for all real $y$, the coefficient of $y^2$ must be negative and the discriminant must be negative.
$m \lt 0$ is required, and the discriminant $D = (6m)^2 - 4(m)(-12) = 36m^2 + 48m$ satisfies $36m^2 + 48m \lt 0$.
Factoring gives $12m(3m + 4) \lt 0$, which holds for $-4/3 \lt m \lt 0$.

Combining both conditions yields the range $-4/3 \lt m \lt 0$.

The correct option is D.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The volume of the tetrahedron whose coterminus edges are represented by $\bar{a}=-12 \hat{i}+\mathrm{p} \hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}=3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-15 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$, is 570 cu. units, then $\mathrm{p}=$
questions.solution:
The volume of a tetrahedron with coterminous edges a, b, c is given by $V = \frac{1}{6} |[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]|$, where $[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]$ is the scalar triple product.

Given vectors: $\bar{a} = (-12, 0, p)$, $\bar{b} = (0, 3, -1)$, $\bar{c} = (2, 1, -15)$, and $V = 570$.

Compute the scalar triple product:
$[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] = \begin{vmatrix} -12 & 0 & p \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -15 \end{vmatrix} = -12 \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & -15 \end{vmatrix} + p \cdot \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$
$= -12 \cdot [3 \cdot (-15) - (-1) \cdot 1] + p \cdot [0 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 2] = 528 - 6p$.

Substitute into the volume formula:
$570 = \frac{1}{6} |528 - 6p|$
$|528 - 6p| = 3420$

This yields two equations:
$528 - 6p = 3420 \implies p = -482$
$528 - 6p = -3420 \implies p = 658$

Among the options, $p = -482$ corresponds to choice C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The length of the altitude through the point D of tetrahedron where the vertices of the tetrahedron are $\mathrm{A}(2,3,1), \mathrm{B}(4,1,-2), \mathrm{C}(6,3,7)$, $D(-5,-4,8)$, is
questions.solution:
The altitude length h through point D is found from the tetrahedron volume formula h = $\frac{3V}{\text{Area}_{\triangle ABC}}$.

Using D as the reference vertex, vectors are computed as:

$\vec{DA} = (7, 7, -7)$
$\vec{DB} = (9, 5, -10)$
$\vec{DC} = (11, 7, -1)$

The scalar triple product gives:

$\vec{DA} \cdot (\vec{DB} \times \vec{DC}) = (7, 7, -7) \cdot (65, -101, 8) = -308$

Thus the volume is $V = \frac{1}{6}|-308| = \frac{154}{3}$.

For the base triangle ABC, vectors from A are:

$\vec{AB} = (2, -2, -3)$
$\vec{AC} = (4, 0, 6)$

The cross product magnitude is $|\vec{AB} \times \vec{AC}| = |(-12, -24, 8)| = 28$, so the area is $\frac{1}{2} \times 28 = 14$.

Substituting into the altitude formula:

$h = \frac{3 \times \frac{154}{3}}{14} = \frac{154}{14} = 11$

The altitude through point D has length 11 units.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The maximum value and minimum value of the volume of the parallelopiped having coterminous edges $\hat{i}+x \hat{j}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \hat{\mathrm{j}}+x \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $x \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ are respectively
questions.solution:
The volume $V$ of the parallelepiped with coterminous edges $\mathrm{a} = \hat{i}+x \hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\mathrm{b} = \hat{j}+x \hat{k}$, and $\mathrm{c} = x \hat{i}+\hat{k}$ is given by the scalar triple product:

$V(x) = |[\mathrm{a} \mathrm{b} \mathrm{c}]| = \left| \begin{vmatrix} 1 & x & 1 \ 0 & 1 & x \ x & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \right|$

Evaluating the determinant yields $V(x) = |x^3 - x + 1|$.

To find the extrema of $V(x)$, consider $f(x) = x^3 - x + 1$ since both critical values are positive. The derivative $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1$ vanishes at $x = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The second derivative $f''(x) = 6x$ shows $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and a local maximum at $x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

At these points:

$f\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = 1 - \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$

$f\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = 1 + \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Both values are positive, so $V(x)$ attains these values directly.

Maximum volume: $1 + \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$

Minimum volume: $1 - \frac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$

These correspond to option B.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{c}$ be unit vectors at an angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ with each other. If $(\bar{a} \times(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})) \cdot(\bar{a} \times \bar{c})=5$, then $\left[\begin{array}{lll}\bar{a} & \bar{b} & \bar{c}\end{array}\right]=$
questions.solution:
The given equation is $(\bar{a} \times(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})) \cdot(\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = 5$.

Using the BAC-CAB identity, $\bar{a} \times(\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})\bar{b} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})\bar{c}$.

Substituting into the original equation yields $[(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})\bar{b} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})\bar{c}] \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = 5$.

Expanding the dot product gives $(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})[\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c})] - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})[\bar{c} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c})] = 5$.

Since $\bar{c} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = 0$ (as two identical vectors in a scalar triple product yield zero), the second term vanishes, simplifying to $(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c})[\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c})] = 5$.

Given $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{c}$ are unit vectors with an angle of $\frac{\pi}{3}$, $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Substituting, $\frac{1}{2}[\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c})] = 5$, so $\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{c}) = 10$.

This expression equals the scalar triple product $[\bar{b} \bar{a} \bar{c}]$, which is related to $[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]$ by a sign change: $[\bar{b} \bar{a} \bar{c}] = -[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}]$.

Thus, $-[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] = 10$, giving $[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] = -10$.

The correct option is B, and the final answer is $\boxed{-10}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}$, and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ be unit vectors. Suppose that $\bar{a} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}=\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c}=0$ and if the angle between $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, then $\bar{a}$ is
questions.solution:
Given that $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ are unit vectors with $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = 0$ and $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{c} = 0$, $\bar{a}$ is perpendicular to both $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$.

Since $\bar{a}$ is orthogonal to $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$, it must be parallel to $\bar{b} \times \bar{c}$, so $\bar{a} = k(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})$ for some scalar $k$.

Using the unit magnitude of $\bar{a}$, $|k||\bar{b} \times \bar{c}| = 1$.

The magnitude $|\bar{b} \times \bar{c}| = |\bar{b}||\bar{c}|\sin\theta = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$.

Thus, $|k|\cdot\frac{1}{2} = 1$, giving $|k| = 2$, so $k = \pm 2$.

Therefore, $\bar{a} = \pm 2(\bar{b} \times \bar{c})$, matching option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ are unit vectors such that $|\bar{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}|=\sqrt{3}$, then the angle between $\bar{a}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ is
questions.solution:
Given that $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ are unit vectors, $|\bar{a}| = |\bar{b}| = 1$. The magnitude of their sum is provided as $|\bar{a} + \bar{b}| = \sqrt{3}$. The magnitude squared is expanded as $|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + 2 \bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}$, leading to $(\sqrt{3})^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 2 \bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}$.

Simplifying, $3 = 2 + 2 \bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}$, so $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = \frac{1}{2}$. Using the dot product definition, $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = |\bar{a}||\bar{b}| \cos \theta = \cos \theta$. Thus, $\cos \theta = \frac{1}{2}$, yielding $\theta = rccos(\frac{1}{2}) = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Three vectors $\hat{i}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \lambda \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+(1-\lambda) \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ and $\mu \hat{i}+\lambda \hat{\mathrm{j}}+(1+\lambda-\mu) \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ represents conterminus edges of a parallelopiped, then the volume of the parallelopiped depends on.
questions.solution:
The volume of the parallelepiped is determined by the scalar triple product of the given vectors:

$\vec{a} = (1, 0, -1)$

$\vec{b} = (\lambda, 1, 1-\lambda)$

$\vec{c} = (\mu, \lambda, 1+\lambda-\mu)$

Evaluating the determinant:

$V = \left| \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ \lambda & 1 & 1-\lambda \\ \mu & \lambda & 1+\lambda-\mu \end{vmatrix} \right|$

Expanding along the first row yields:

$V = \left| (1+\lambda-\mu - \lambda + \lambda^2) - (\lambda^2 - \mu) \right| = \left| 1 \right| = 1$

The volume simplifies to a constant value of 1, independent of both $\lambda$ and $\mu$.

Therefore, the volume depends on neither parameter.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{D}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The lines $\overline{\mathrm{r}}=\bar{a}+\lambda(\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})$ and $\overline{\mathrm{r}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}}+\lambda(\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}})$ will intersect if
questions.solution:
Given lines:
$L_1: \vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$
$L_2: \vec{r} = \vec{c} + \mu (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$

For intersection, there exist $\lambda$, $\mu$ such that $\vec{a} + \lambda (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{c} + \mu (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})$.

Dot both sides with $\vec{b}$:

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} + \lambda [\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})] = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c} + \mu [\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{a} \times \vec{b})]$

Since scalar triple products with repeated vectors vanish,

$\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$

This is necessary for intersection.

The general intersection condition is $(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{d}_1 \times \vec{d}_2) = 0$. Here, $\vec{a}_1 = \vec{a}$, $\vec{d}_1 = \vec{b} \times \vec{c}$, $\vec{a}_2 = \vec{c}$, $\vec{d}_2 = \vec{a} \times \vec{b}$.

Compute $(\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \times (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) = -[\vec{a} \vec{b} \vec{c}] \vec{b}$ using vector triple product identity.

The condition becomes:

$(\vec{c} - \vec{a}) \cdot \left(-[\vec{a} \vec{b} \vec{c}] \vec{b}\right) = 0$

$-[\vec{a} \vec{b} \vec{c}] (\vec{c} \cdot \vec{b} - \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) = 0$

This holds if $[\vec{a} \vec{b} \vec{c}] = 0$ or $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{c} \cdot \vec{b}$.

Since $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$ is both necessary and sufficient, it is the required condition.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: In a triangle ABC with usual notations if $|\overline{\mathrm{BC}}|=8,|\overline{\mathrm{CA}}|=7,|\overline{\mathrm{AB}}|=10$ then the projection of $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}$ on $\overline{\mathrm{AC}}$ is
questions.solution:
The projection of $\overline{AB}$ onto $\overline{AC}$ is given by $\frac{\overline{AB} \cdot \overline{AC}}{|\overline{AC}|}$.

Using the law of cosines to find the angle between the vectors: $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$ where $a = 8$, $b = 7$, and $c = 10$.
This yields $64 = 49 + 100 - 140\cos A$, so $140\cos A = 85$ and $\cos A = \frac{85}{140}$.

The dot product becomes $\overline{AB} \cdot \overline{AC} = |\overline{AB}||\overline{AC}|\cos A = 70 \cdot \frac{85}{140} = \frac{85}{2}$.

Substituting into the projection formula: $\frac{85/2}{7} = \frac{85}{14}$.

The projection length is $\frac{85}{14}$, matching option C.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the projection of $\bar{a}$ on $\bar{b}+\bar{c}$ is twice the projection of $\bar{b}+\bar{c}$ on $\bar{a}$ also if $|\bar{b}|=2 \sqrt{2},|\bar{c}|=4$ and the angle between $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$ is $\frac{\pi}{4}$ then $|\bar{a}|=$
questions.solution:
The projection of $\bar{a}$ on $(\bar{b}+\bar{c})$ is twice that of $(\bar{b}+\bar{c})$ on $\bar{a}$, yielding the relation:

$\frac{\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b}+\bar{c})}{|\bar{b}+\bar{c}|} = 2 \cdot \frac{\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b}+\bar{c})}{|\bar{a}|}$

Canceling the common nonzero dot product and simplifying gives:

$|\bar{a}| = 2 |\bar{b}+\bar{c}|$

The magnitude of $\bar{b}+\bar{c}$ is computed using the given data: $|\bar{b}| = 2\sqrt{2}$, $|\bar{c}| = 4$, and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$.

$|\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 = |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 + 2 \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} = (2\sqrt{2})^2 + 4^2 + 2 \cdot (2\sqrt{2} \cdot 4 \cdot \cos\frac{\pi}{4})$

$|\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 = 8 + 16 + 2 (8\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}) = 24 + 16 = 40$

Thus $|\bar{b}+\bar{c}| = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}$, and substituting into the earlier relation gives:

$|\bar{a}| = 2 \cdot 2\sqrt{10} = 4\sqrt{10}$

Answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If the points $\mathrm{A}(1,1,2), \mathrm{B}(2,1, \mathrm{p}), \mathrm{C}(1,0,3)$ and $\mathrm{D}(2,2,0)$ are coplanar then the value of $p$ is
questions.solution:
Four points are coplanar if the scalar triple product of vectors from one point to the other three is zero.

From point A(1,1,2), the vectors are:

$\vec{AB} = (1, 0, p-2)$

$\vec{AC} = (0, -1, 1)$

$\vec{AD} = (1, 1, -2)$

The scalar triple product $[\vec{AB} \vec{AC} \vec{AD}]$ equals the determinant:

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 & p-2 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Evaluating the determinant yields:

$1 \cdot (2 - 1) + (p-2) \cdot (0 + 1) = 0$

$1 + p - 2 = 0$

$p = 1$

The points are coplanar when $p = 1$, corresponding to option C.

questions.q: If $\bar{a}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ are unit vectors and $\theta$ is the angle between them, then $\tan \theta / 2=$
questions.solution:
Given that $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ are unit vectors, with angle $\theta$ between them, their dot product yields $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = \cos\theta$.

Evaluating $|\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2$ using vector algebra:

$|\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2 = 2(1 - \cos\theta) = 4\sin^2(\theta/2)$

Hence, $|\bar{a} - \bar{b}| = 2\sin(\theta/2)$ for $\theta \in [0, \pi]$.

Similarly for $|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|^2$:

$|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|^2 = 2(1 + \cos\theta) = 4\cos^2(\theta/2)$

Thus, $|\bar{a} + \bar{b}| = 2\cos(\theta/2)$.

Taking the ratio yields the tangent of the half-angle:

$\tan(\theta/2) = \frac{|\bar{a} - \bar{b}|}{|\bar{a} + \bar{b}|}$

This result corresponds to option D.

questions.q: If $\overline{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3 \hat{i}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{1}{7}(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-6 \hat{\mathrm{k}})$ then the value of $(2 \bar{a}-\bar{b}) \cdot[(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times(\bar{a}+2 \bar{b})]=$
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3\hat{i} + \hat{k})$ and $\bar{b} = \frac{1}{7}(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k})$, both have unit magnitude since $|\bar{a}| = 1$ and $|\bar{b}| = 1$. Their dot product $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = 0$, confirming orthogonality.

The expression $(2\bar{a} - \bar{b}) \cdot [(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times (\bar{a} + 2\bar{b})]$ simplifies using the vector triple product identity. For orthogonal unit vectors, $(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times \bar{a} = \bar{b}$ and $(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times \bar{b} = -\bar{a}$, yielding $(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times (\bar{a} + 2\bar{b}) = \bar{b} - 2\bar{a}$.

The dot product becomes $(2\bar{a} - \bar{b}) \cdot (\bar{b} - 2\bar{a}) = -|2\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2$. Since $|2\bar{a} - \bar{b}|^2 = 4|\bar{a}|^2 - 4(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + |\bar{b}|^2 = 4 + 0 + 1 = 5$, the expression evaluates to $-5$.

Final answer: $\boxed{-5}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ be two vectors such that. $|\bar{a}|=1,|\bar{b}|=4, \bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}=2$. If $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=(2 \bar{a} \times \bar{b})-3 \bar{b}$, then the angle between $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ with $|\bar{a}|=1$, $|\bar{b}|=4$, and $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}=2$, and $\bar{c} = (2\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) - 3\bar{b}$, the angle $\theta$ between $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$ is determined.

The dot product $\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c}$ evaluates to $2[\bar{b} \cdot (\bar{a} \times \bar{b})] - 3(\bar{b} \cdot \bar{b})$. The scalar triple product $[\bar{b}, \bar{a}, \bar{b}]$ is zero, simplifying to $\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} = -3|\bar{b}|^2 = -48$.

To compute $|\bar{c}|$, expand $|\bar{c}|^2 = |2\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|^2 + |-3\bar{b}|^2 - 2((2\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot (3\bar{b}))$. The scalar triple product term is zero, yielding $|\bar{c}|^2 = 4|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|^2 + 9|\bar{b}|^2$. Using $|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2|\bar{b}|^2 - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})^2 = 12$, we find $|\bar{c}|^2 = 4(12) + 9(16) = 192$, so $|\bar{c}| = 8\sqrt{3}$.

The cosine of the angle is $\cos \theta = \frac{\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c}}{|\bar{b}||\bar{c}|} = \frac{-48}{(4)(8\sqrt{3})} = \frac{-3}{2\sqrt{3}} = \frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}$. This corresponds to $\theta = \frac{5\pi}{6}$.

The answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}, \bar{d}$ are unit vectors such that $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}=\frac{1}{2}, \bar{c} \cdot \bar{d}=\frac{1}{2}$ and the angle between $\bar{a} \times \bar{b}$ and $\bar{c} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}}$ is $\frac{\pi}{6}$, then the value of $|[\bar{a} \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \mathrm{~d}] \bar{c}-[\bar{a} \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \bar{c}] \mathrm{d}|=$
questions.solution:
Given $E = |[\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{d}] \bar{c} - [\bar{a} \bar{b} \bar{c}] \bar{d}|$, express the scalar triple products using cross and dot products:

$E = |((\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot \bar{d}) \bar{c} - ((\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \cdot \bar{c}) \bar{d}|$.

This matches the vector triple product identity $\bar{X} \times (\bar{Y} \times \bar{Z}) = (\bar{X} \cdot \bar{Z})\bar{Y} - (\bar{X} \cdot \bar{Y})\bar{Z}$, with $\bar{X} = \bar{a} \times \bar{b}$, $\bar{Y} = \bar{c}$, and $\bar{Z} = \bar{d}$. Thus, $E = |(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times (\bar{c} \times \bar{d})|$.

Let $\bar{P} = \bar{a} \times \bar{b}$ and $\bar{Q} = \bar{c} \times \bar{d}$. Then $E = |\bar{P} \times \bar{Q}| = |\bar{P}||\bar{Q}|\sin\phi$, where $\phi = \frac{\pi}{6}$ is given, so $\sin\phi = \frac{1}{2}$.

The magnitudes are computed similarly: $|\bar{a} \times \bar{b}| = |\bar{a}||\bar{b}|\sin\theta_1 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \sin(\frac{\pi}{3}) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, since $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = \frac{1}{2}$ implies $\theta_1 = \frac{\pi}{3}$.

Likewise, $|\bar{c} \times \bar{d}| = |\bar{c}||\bar{d}|\sin\theta_2 = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \sin(\frac{\pi}{3}) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Substituting, $E = \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{3}{8}$.

The correct answer is C.

questions.q: $\begin{aligned} & \text { If } \bar{a}=4 \hat{i}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}, \quad \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\hat{i}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \text { then } \bar{a} \times(\bar{a} \times(\bar{a} \times(\bar{a} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}})))=\end{aligned}$
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\bar{b} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, the dot product is $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = (4)(1) + (3)(-2) + (1)(2) = 0$, confirming orthogonality.

The magnitude squared is $|\bar{a}|^2 = 4^2 + 3^2 + 1^2 = 26$.

Evaluating the nested cross product $\bar{a} \times (\bar{a} \times (\bar{a} \times (\bar{a} \times \bar{b})))$
Using the vector triple product identity $\bar{x} \times (\bar{y} \times \bar{z}) = (\bar{x} \cdot \bar{z})\bar{y} - (\bar{x} \cdot \bar{y})\bar{z}$:

Let $\bar{v}_2 = \bar{a} \times (\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) = (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b})\bar{a} - (\bar{a} \cdot \bar{a})\bar{b} = -26\bar{b}$.

Then $\bar{v}_3 = \bar{a} \times \bar{v}_2 = \bar{a} \times (-26\bar{b}) = -26(\bar{a} \times \bar{b})$.

Finally, $\bar{v}_4 = \bar{a} \times \bar{v}_3 = \bar{a} \times (-26\bar{v}_1) = -26(\bar{a} \times \bar{v}_1) = -26(-26\bar{b}) = 676\bar{b}$.

The result simplifies to $676\bar{b}$.

questions.q: If $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ are unit vectors and $\theta$ is the angle between them, then $\bar{a}+\bar{b}$ is a unit vector when $\theta$ is
questions.solution:
Given unit vectors $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$, where $\left|\bar{a}\right| = 1$ and $\left|\bar{b}\right| = 1$, and $\left|\bar{a} + \bar{b}\right| = 1$.

The magnitude squared expands to $\left|\bar{a} + \bar{b}\right|^{2} = \left|\bar{a}\right|^{2} + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + \left|\bar{b}\right|^{2}$.

Substituting known values gives $1 = 1 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + 1$, which simplifies to $2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) = -1$, so $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = -\frac{1}{2}$.

Using the dot product formula $\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} = \left|\bar{a}\right| \left|\bar{b}\right| \cos\theta = \cos\theta$, we find $\cos\theta = -\frac{1}{2}$, yielding $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.

Correct option: B

questions.q: The magnitude of a vector which is orthogonal to the vector $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and is coplanar with the vectors $\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ is
questions.solution:
Let v be a vector orthogonal to a = $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, so v · a = 0, and coplanar with b = $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and c = $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

Since v is orthogonal to a and coplanar with b and c, it must be parallel to a × (b × c). First, calculate b × c:

$\hat{i}(1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2) - \hat{j}(1 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 1) + \hat{k}(1 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1)$
= $-3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$

Then evaluate the cross product a × (b × c):

$\hat{i}(1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1) - \hat{j}(1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot (-3)) + \hat{k}(1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot (-3))$
= $0\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$

Thus, v is proportional to $-4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, which has magnitude

$\sqrt{(-4)^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{32} = 4\sqrt{2}$

The correct option is B.

questions.q: Let $\overline{\mathrm{OA}}=\overline{\mathrm{a}}, \overline{\mathrm{OB}}=\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and if the vector along the angle bisector of $\angle \mathrm{AOB}$ is given by $x \frac{\overline{\mathrm{a}}}{|\overline{\mathrm{a}}|}+\mathrm{y} \frac{\overline{\mathrm{b}}}{|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|}$ then
questions.solution:
Let a and b represent the vectors $\overline{OA}$ and $\overline{OB}$ respectively.

The angle bisector direction is given by the sum of the unit vectors: $\frac{\overline{a}}{|\overline{a}|} + \frac{\overline{b}}{|\overline{b}|}$.

Comparing with the given expression $x\frac{\overline{a}}{|\overline{a}|} + y\frac{\overline{b}}{|\overline{b}|}$, the coefficients must be equal since the unit vectors are linearly independent.

Therefore $x = y$, or equivalently $x - y = 0$.

$x - y = 0$

The correct option is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.q: In triangle ABC , the point P divides BC internally in the ratio $3: 4$ and Q divides CA internally in the ratio $5: 3$. If AP and BQ intersect in a point $G$, then $G$ divides $A P$ internally in the ratio
questions.solution:
Given triangle ABC with point $P$ on $BC$ dividing it $3:4$ so $BP:PC = 3:4$ and point $Q$ on $CA$ dividing it $5:3$ so $CQ:QA = 5:3$, determine the ratio $AG:GP$ using Menelaus’ Theorem.

Apply Menelaus’ Theorem to $\triangle ACP$ with transversal $B-G-Q$:

$\frac{AQ}{QC} \cdot \frac{CB}{BP} \cdot \frac{PG}{GA} = 1$

Substitute the given ratios:

From $CQ:QA = 5:3$, $\frac{AQ}{QC} = \frac{3}{5}$

From $BP:PC = 3:4$, $BC = BP + PC = 3k + 4k = 7k$ for some $k$, so $\frac{CB}{BP} = \frac{7}{3}$

Thus,

$\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)\frac{PG}{GA} = 1$

$\frac{7}{5} \cdot \frac{PG}{GA} = 1$

$\frac{PG}{GA} = \frac{5}{7}$

Since $\frac{AG}{GP} = \frac{7}{5}$, point $G$ divides $AP$ internally in the ratio $7:5$.

Final answer: $\boxed{C}$

questions.q: Let $\overline{\mathrm{u}}, \overline{\mathrm{v}}, \overline{\mathrm{w}}$ be the vectors such that $|\overline{\mathrm{u}}|=1,|\overline{\mathrm{v}}|=2,|\overline{\mathrm{w}}|=3$. If the projection $\overline{\mathrm{v}}$ along $\overline{\mathrm{u}}$ is equal to that of $\overline{\mathrm{w}}$ along $\overline{\mathrm{u}}$ and the vectors $\overline{\mathrm{v}}$, $\overline{\mathrm{w}}$ are perpendicular to each other then $|\overline{\mathrm{u}}-\overline{\mathrm{v}}+\overline{\mathrm{w}}|$ equals
questions.solution:
Given vectors u, v, w with magnitudes $|\overline{\mathrm{u}}|=1$, $|\overline{\mathrm{v}}|=2$, $|\overline{\mathrm{w}}|=3$, and conditions that the projection of v and w along u are equal, and that v and w are perpendicular.

The projection equality implies $\frac{\overline{\mathrm{v}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{u}}}{|\overline{\mathrm{u}}|} = \frac{\overline{\mathrm{w}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{u}}}{|\overline{\mathrm{u}}|}$, so $\overline{\mathrm{v}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{u}} = \overline{\mathrm{w}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{u}}$.
Since $\overline{\mathrm{v}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{w}} = 0$, we compute the squared magnitude:

$|\overline{\mathrm{u}}-\overline{\mathrm{v}}+\overline{\mathrm{w}}|^2 = (\overline{\mathrm{u}}-\overline{\mathrm{v}}+\overline{\mathrm{w}}) \cdot (\overline{\mathrm{u}}-\overline{\mathrm{v}}+\overline{\mathrm{w}})$
$= |\overline{\mathrm{u}}|^2 + |\overline{\mathrm{v}}|^2 + |\overline{\mathrm{w}}|^2 - 2(\overline{\mathrm{u}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{v}}) + 2(\overline{\mathrm{u}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{w}}) - 2(\overline{\mathrm{v}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{w}})$
$= 1 + 4 + 9 - 2(\overline{\mathrm{u}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{v}}) + 2(\overline{\mathrm{u}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{v}}) - 0 = 14$

Thus $|\overline{\mathrm{u}}-\overline{\mathrm{v}}+\overline{\mathrm{w}}| = \sqrt{14}$, matching option A.

questions.q: If $\bar{a}, \bar{b}, \bar{c}$ are three vectors such that $\overline{|a|}=3, \overline{|b|}=5, \overline{|c|}=7$ then $|\bar{a}-\bar{b}|^2+|\bar{b}-\bar{c}|^2+|\bar{c}-\bar{a}|^2$ does not exceed
questions.solution:
Given vectors $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ with magnitudes $|\bar{a}| = 3$, $|\bar{b}| = 5$, and $|\bar{c}| = 7$, we compute $E = |\bar{a}-\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{b}-\bar{c}|^2 + |\bar{c}-\bar{a}|^2$.

Using the identity $|\bar{x}-\bar{y}|^2 = |\bar{x}|^2 + |\bar{y}|^2 - 2\bar{x} \cdot \bar{y}$, we expand:

$E = (|\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 - 2\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b}) + (|\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 - 2\bar{b} \cdot \bar{c}) + (|\bar{c}|^2 + |\bar{a}|^2 - 2\bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$

Summing terms yields $E = 2(|\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2) - 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$.

With $|\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 = 9 + 25 + 49 = 83$, we have $E = 166 - 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$.

From $|\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 = |\bar{a}|^2 + |\bar{b}|^2 + |\bar{c}|^2 + 2(\bar{a} \cdot \bar{b} + \bar{b} \cdot \bar{c} + \bar{c} \cdot \bar{a})$, we substitute:

$E = 2(83) - [|\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 - 83] = 249 - |\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2$.

Since $|\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2 \geq 0$, $E$ is maximized when $|\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c}|^2$ is minimized. The minimum value of $0$ is attainable because the vectors with magnitudes $3$, $5$, and $7$ satisfy the triangle inequalities: $3+5 \gt 7$, $3+7 \gt 5$, and $5+7 \gt 3$, confirming that $\bar{a}+\bar{b}+\bar{c} = \bar{0}$ is possible.

Thus, $E_{\text{max}} = 249 - 0 = 249$.

The maximum value is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

questions.q: The volume of the tetrahedron whose co-terminus edges are $\bar{a}, \overline{\mathrm{~b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is 12 cubic units. If the scalar projection of $\bar{a}$ on $\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is 4 , then $|\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}|=$
questions.solution:
The volume of a tetrahedron with coterminous edges $\bar{a}$, $\bar{b}$, and $\bar{c}$ is given by $V = \frac{1}{6} |\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b} \times \bar{c})|$.

Given $V = 12$ yields $|\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b} \times \bar{c})| = 72$.

The scalar projection of $\bar{a}$ on $\bar{b} \times \bar{c}$ is $\frac{\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b} \times \bar{c})}{|\bar{b} \times \bar{c}|} = 4$, so $\bar{a} \cdot (\bar{b} \times \bar{c}) = 4 |\bar{b} \times \bar{c}|$.

Substituting into the volume expression gives $4 |\bar{b} \times \bar{c}| = 72$, hence $|\bar{b} \times \bar{c}| = 18$.

Answer: $18$

If $\theta$ is the angle between vectors $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$, then the value of $\sin \theta$ is
questions.solution:
Given, $(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{1}{3}|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}||\overline{\mathrm{c}}| \overline{\mathrm{a}}$ We know that, $(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{b}}-(\overline{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}$
On comparing, we get $\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{3}|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}||\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=-\overline{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}||\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=-|\overline{\mathrm{b}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{c}}| \cos \theta \\ & \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{-1}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \cos ^2 \theta=\frac{1}{9} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \sin ^2 \theta & =1-\cos ^2 \theta \\ & =1-\frac{1}{9} \\ \therefore \quad \sin ^2 \theta & =\frac{8}{9} \\ \therefore \quad \sin \theta & =\sqrt{\frac{8}{9}}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Let $A D$ be the median of $\triangle A B C$.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \overline{\mathrm{AD}} & =\frac{\overline{\mathrm{AB}}+\overline{\mathrm{AC}}}{2} \\
& =\frac{3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{k}}+5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{k}}}{2} \\
& =\frac{8 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+8 \hat{\mathrm{k}}}{2} \\
& =4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\

questions.solution:
Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$.
Since $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\overline{\mathrm{a}}+2 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{d}}=5 \overline{\mathrm{a}}-4 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}$ are perpendicular to each other.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \overline{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~d}}=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+2 \overline{\mathrm{~b}}) \cdot(5 \overline{\mathrm{a}}-4 \overline{\mathrm{~b}})=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 5(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{a}})+6(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}})-8(\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}})=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 5|\overline{\mathrm{a}}|^2+6|\overline{\mathrm{a}}||\overline{\mathrm{b}}| \cos \theta-8|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}|^2=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 5+6 \cos \theta-8=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}
\end{aligned}$

In $\triangle \mathrm{ABC}$, $\begin{aligned} & \overline{\mathrm{a}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}}=\overline{\overline{\mathrm{c}}} \ldots \ldots[\text { Using triangle law of addition] } \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{b}} & =\overline{\mathrm{c}}-\overline{\mathrm{a}} \\ & =2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}-(3 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}})=-\hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ \overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}} & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{\mathrm{i}} & \hat{\mathrm{j}} & \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{array}\right|=-\hat{\mathrm{i}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \text { Area of parallelogram } & =|\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}| \\ & =\sqrt{1+16+1} \\ & =\sqrt{18}=3 \sqrt{2} \text { sq. units } \end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Given: - $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$, - $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$, - Find $\mathbf{b}$ such that $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})+\mathbf{c}=0$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{3}$.
Write b in component form: $\mathbf{b}=p \mathbf{i}+q \mathbf{j}+r \mathbf{k}$
Compute $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ : $\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} & =(0,1,-1), \quad \mathbf{b}=(p, q, r) \\ \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ p & q & r \end{array}\right| & =\mathbf{i}(1 r-(-1) q)-\mathbf{j}(0 r-(-1) p)+\mathbf{k}(0 q-1 p) \\ \mathbf{a} & \times \mathbf{b}=(r+q) \mathbf{i}-(-p) \mathbf{j}-p \mathbf{k} \\ \mathbf{a} & \times \mathbf{b}=(r+q) \mathbf{i}+p \mathbf{j}-p \mathbf{k} \end{aligned}$
Use $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})+\mathbf{c}=0$ : $(r+q) \mathbf{i}+p \mathbf{j}-p \mathbf{k}+(\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k})=0$
Equating components: - $i$-component: $r+q+1=0 \Rightarrow r+q=-1$, - $j$-component: $p-1=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad p=1$, - $k$-component: $-p-1=0 \Rightarrow p=-1$.
Solve $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=3$ : $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=(0) p+(1) q+(-1) r=q-r=3$
From $r+q=-1$ and $q-r=3$, solve for $q$ and $r$ : - Add equations: $2 q=2 \Rightarrow q=1$, - Substitute: $r+1=-1 \Rightarrow r=-2$.
Final b: $\mathbf{b}=-\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$
Answer: $\mathbf{- i}+\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}$.

questions.q: The vector $\overline{\mathrm{a}}=\alpha \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\beta \hat{\mathrm{k}}$ lies in the plane of the vectors $\bar{b}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}$ and $\bar{c}=\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and bisects the angle between $\bar{b}$ and $\bar{c}$. Then which one of the following gives possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ ?
questions.solution:
Since $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ bisects the angle between $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$. $\therefore \quad$ The equation of bisector of $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is $\begin{aligned} & \overline{\mathrm{a}}=\lambda(\hat{\mathrm{b}}+\hat{\mathrm{c}}) \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\beta \hat{\mathrm{k}}=\lambda\left(\frac{\hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \end{aligned}\Rightarrow \alpha \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\beta \hat{\mathrm{k}}=\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})$
On comparing, we get $\alpha=\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2}}, 2=\sqrt{2} \lambda$ and $\beta=\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{2}}\Rightarrow \alpha=1, \beta=1$

Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\hat{a}$ and $\hat{b}$.
Since $\bar{c}=\hat{a}+2 \hat{b}$ and $\bar{d}=5 \hat{a}+4 \hat{b}$ are perpendicular to each other.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \overline{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{~d}}=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(\hat{\mathrm{a}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{~b}}) \cdot(5 \hat{\mathrm{a}}+4 \hat{\mathrm{~b}})=0 \\

questions.q: If the vectors $a \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{i}+b \hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{i}+\hat{j}+c \hat{k}(a \neq b, c \neq 1)$ are coplanar, then $\frac{1}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}$ has the value $\qquad$
questions.solution:
Since $\left|\begin{array}{lll}a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & b & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & c\end{array}\right|=0$ Applying $\mathrm{R}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_2-\mathrm{R}_1$ and $\mathrm{R}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{R}_3-\mathrm{R}_1$, we get $\begin{aligned} & \left|\begin{array}{ccc} a & 1 & 1 \\ 1-a & b-1 & 0 \\ 1-a & 0 & c-1 \end{array}\right|=0 \\ & \Rightarrow a(b-1)(c-1)-(1-a)(c-1)-(1-a)(b-1)=0 \end{aligned}$
Dividing by $(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)$, we get $\frac{a}{1-a}+\frac{1}{1-b}+\frac{1}{1-c}=0$ Consider, $\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{a}}+\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{b}}+\frac{1}{1-\mathrm{c}}=\frac{1}{1-a}-\frac{a}{1-a}$ ....[From (i)] $=1$

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & {[\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}] \cdot[(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}})]} \\ & =(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \cdot[(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}})]+\overline{\mathrm{c}} \cdot[(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times(\overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}})] \\ & =0+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}] \\ & =[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}]+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}}] \\ & =[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}]+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}]+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}] \\ & =0+0+[\overline{\mathrm{c}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{a}}]+0 \\ & =-[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Suppose that $\bar{p}, \bar{q}$ and $\bar{r}$ are three non-coplanar vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let the components of a vector $\bar{s}$ along $\bar{p}, \bar{q}$ and $\bar{r}$ be 4,3 and 5 respectively. If the components of this vector $\overline{\mathrm{s}}$ along $(-\overline{\mathrm{p}}+\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}}),(\overline{\mathrm{p}}-\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}})$ and $(-\overline{\mathrm{p}}-\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}})$ are $x$, $y$ and $z$ respectively, then the value of $2 x+y+z$ is
questions.solution:
Given
$\begin{aligned}
& \overline{\mathrm{s}}=4 \overline{\mathrm{p}}+3 \overline{\mathrm{q}}+5 \overline{\mathrm{r}} \\
& \mathrm{~s}=(-\overline{\mathrm{p}}+\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}}) x+(\overline{\mathrm{p}}-\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}}) y+(-\overline{\mathrm{p}}-\overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{r}}) \mathrm{z} \\
& \begin{aligned}
& 4 \overline{\mathrm{p}}+3 \overline{\mathrm{q}}+5 \overline{\mathrm{r}}=(-x+y-\mathrm{z}) \overline{\mathrm{p}}+(x-y-\mathrm{z}) \overline{\mathrm{q}} \\
&+(x+y+\mathrm{z}) \overline{\mathrm{r}}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}$
Comparing, we get
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & -x+y-z=4 ...(i)\\
& x-y-z=3 ...(ii)\\
& x+y+z=5
...(iii)\end{aligned}$
Solving (i), (ii) and (iii), we get
$x=4, y=\frac{9}{2}, z=\frac{-7}{2}\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad 2 x+y+z & =2(4)+\frac{9}{2}-\frac{7}{2} \\
& =2(4)+1 \\
& =9
\end{aligned}$

Now, $|(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times \bar{c}|=|\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}| \cdot|\overline{\mathrm{c}}| \sin 60^{\circ}\begin{aligned} & =(3)(1)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ & =\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$ ...[From (i) and (ii)]

questions.q: If $\overline{\mathrm{a}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}, \overline{\mathrm{c}}$ are non-coplanar vectors and $\overline{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}}{[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]}, \overline{\mathrm{q}}=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{c}} \times \overline{\mathrm{a}}}{[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]}, \overline{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}}{[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]}, \quad$ then $2 \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{p}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{q}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{r}}=$

& 2 \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{2(\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \cdot \overline{\mathrm{a}}}{[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]}=\frac{2[\overline{\mathrm{~b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{a}]}{[\overline{\mathrm{a}} \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \overline{\mathrm{c}}]}=2 . \\

Let $\bar{a}=\alpha \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}-\hat{k}, \bar{b}=3 \hat{i}-\beta \hat{j}+4 \hat{k} \quad$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$, where $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$, be three vectors.
If the projection of $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ on $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is $\frac{10}{3}$ and $\bar{b} \times \bar{c}=-6 \hat{i}+10 \hat{j}+7 \hat{k}$, then the value of $2 \alpha+\beta$ is
questions.solution:
Projection of $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ on $\overline{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}}{|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|}\begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad \frac{\alpha+6+2}{\sqrt{1+4+4}}=\frac{10}{3} \\ & \therefore \quad \alpha=2 \\ & \overline{\mathbf{b}} \times \overline{\mathbf{c}}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 3 & -\beta & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & -2 \end{array}\right| \\ & =(2 \beta-8) \hat{i}-(-6-4) \hat{j}+(6+\beta) \hat{k} \\ & =(2 \beta-8) \hat{i}+10 \hat{j}+(6+\beta) \hat{k} \end{aligned}$
Comparing with $-6 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+10 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+7 \hat{\mathrm{k}}$, we get $\begin{array}{ll} & 2 \beta-8=-6 \\ \therefore & 2 \beta=2 \\ \therefore \quad & \beta=1 \\ \therefore \quad & 2 \alpha+\beta=5 \end{array}$

$\therefore \quad \overline{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{p}+2 \mathrm{q}}{3+2}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{3 \mathrm{p}-2 \mathrm{q}}{3-2}$

questions.q: The value of a for which the volume of parallelepiped formed by $\hat{i}+a \hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{j}+a \hat{k}$ and $a \hat{i}+\hat{k}$ becomes minimum is
questions.solution:
i.e., $V=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & a & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & a \\ a & 0 & 1\end{array}\right| \doteq 1-a+a^3\therefore \quad \frac{d V}{d a}=-1+3 a^2, \frac{d^2 V}{d a^2}=6 a$
For max. or min. of $V, \frac{d V}{d a}=0\therefore \quad \mathrm{a}^2=\frac{1}{3}\therefore \quad a=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of distinct real values of $\lambda$, for which the vectors $-\lambda^2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}, \hat{i}-\lambda^2 \hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\lambda^2 \hat{k}$ are coplanar, is
questions.solution:
For co-planar vectors, we have
$\begin{aligned}
& \left|\begin{array}{ccc}
-\lambda^2 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & -\lambda^2 & 1 \\
1 & 1 & -\lambda^2
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \therefore \quad-\lambda^2\left(\lambda^4-1\right)-1\left(-\lambda^2-1\right)+1\left(1+\lambda^2\right)=0 \\
& \therefore \quad-\lambda^6+\lambda^2+\lambda^2+1+1+\lambda^2=0 \\
& \therefore \quad \lambda^6-3 \lambda^2-2=0 \\
& \therefore \quad t^3-3 t-2=0 \\
& \ldots\left[\text { For } \mathrm{t}=\lambda^2\right] \\
& \therefore \quad(\mathrm{t}+1)\left(\mathrm{t}^2-\mathrm{t}-2\right)=0 \\
& \therefore \quad(\mathrm{t}+1)(\mathrm{t}+1)(\mathrm{t}-2)=0 \\
& \therefore \quad t=-1 \text { or } t=2 \\
& \text { i.e., } \lambda^2=-1 \text { or } \lambda^2=2
\end{aligned}$
for real values of $\lambda$, we get $\lambda= \pm \sqrt{2}$, two values.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $\overline{\mathrm{a}}, \overline{\mathrm{b}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ be three vectors having magnitude 1,1 and 2 respectively. If $\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})+\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{0}$, then the acute angle between $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ is
questions.solution:
Given, $|\bar{a}|=1,|\bar{b}|=1$ and $|\bar{c}|=2\begin{aligned}
& \text { Also, } \overline{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})+\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{0} \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{a}}) \overline{\mathrm{c}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}} \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}-\overline{\mathrm{c}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}=\overline{0} \quad \quad \ldots\left[\because \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{a}}=|\overline{\mathrm{a}}|^2=1\right] \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}-\overline{\mathrm{c}}=-\overline{\mathrm{b}} \\
& \Rightarrow|(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}-\overline{\mathrm{c}}|=|-\overline{\mathrm{b}}| \\
& \Rightarrow\left|(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})^{\overline{\mathrm{a}}-\overline{\mathrm{c}}}\right|^2=|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2 \\
& \Rightarrow|(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}}|^2+|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2-2\{(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}\}=|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2 \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})^2|\overline{\mathrm{a}}|^2+|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2-2(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})=|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2 \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})^2\left\{|\overline{\mathrm{a}}|^2-2\right\}+|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2=|\overline{\mathrm{b}}|^2
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})^2+4=1 \quad \ldots\left[\because|\overline{\mathrm{~b}}|^2=1,|\overline{\mathrm{c}}|^2=4\right] \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}})^2=3 \\
& \Rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}= \pm \sqrt{3} \\
& \Rightarrow|\overline{\mathrm{a}}||\overline{\mathrm{c}}| \cos \theta=\sqrt{3}
\end{aligned}$
where $\theta$ is an acute angle between $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}\Rightarrow \cos \theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The vectors $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ are not perpendicular and $\overline{\mathrm{c}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{d}}$ are two vectors satisfying $\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{d}}=0$, then the vector $\overline{\mathrm{d}}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,
Vectors $\overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ are not perpendicular
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \neq 0 \\
& \overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~d}}=0 \\
& \overline{\mathrm{~b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}}=\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}} \\
& \Rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{c}})=\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times(\overline{\mathrm{b}} \times \overline{\mathrm{d}}) \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{b}}-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}) \overline{\mathrm{c}}=(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~d}}) \overline{\mathrm{b}}-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}) \overline{\mathrm{d}} \\
& \Rightarrow(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}) \overline{\mathrm{d}}=-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \cdot \overline{\mathrm{b}}+(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}) \overline{\mathrm{c}} \\
\quad & \Rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{~d}}=\frac{-(\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}) \overline{\mathrm{b}}}{\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}}+\overline{\mathrm{c}} \\
\Rightarrow & \overline{\mathrm{~d}}=\overline{\mathrm{c}}-\left(\frac{\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{c}}}{\overline{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overline{\mathrm{~b}}}\right) \overline{\mathrm{b}}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If $\overline{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}), \overline{\mathrm{b}}=\frac{1}{5}(\hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{k}})$, then the value of $(2 \bar{a}-\bar{b}) \cdot\{(\bar{a} \times \bar{b}) \times(\bar{a}+2 \bar{b})\}$ is
questions.solution:
$\therefore \quad \overline{\mathrm{a}}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{b}}$ are perpendicular unit vectors.
$\begin{aligned}
